batchName: Empire: Tiberius and Caligula (AD 14-41) - Hard Batch 1

questions.question: When a shoemaker from Gaul called Caligula "a complete idiot", how did the emperor react?
options: He had the man executed on the spot
He fined him a year's earnings
He exiled him back to Gaul
He made him a senator as a joke
He had him thrown into the Tiber
He seemed to appreciate the honesty
questions.explanation: Caligula apparently enjoyed the shoemaker's frankness. The same emperor liked to dress as gods, including Jupiter.
questions.sourceQuote: When a shoemaker from Gaul called him "a complete idiot", Caligula seemed to appreciate the honesty.

questions.question: How long after Caligula's death did his main ancient biographer write?
options: 120 years
250 years
80 years
20 years
180 years
40 years
questions.explanation: Caligula's main biographer wrote about 80 years after his death, and another historian more than 180 years after. No surviving source is friendly to him.
questions.sourceQuote: His main biographer wrote 80 years after his death, another historian over 180 years after, and no surviving source is friendly.

questions.question: What finally led Augustus to turn back to Tiberius after his retirement to Rhodes?
options: The deaths of Augustus's two young grandsons and heirs
The death of Germanicus at Antioch
A mutiny of the Rhine legions
Tiberius's divorce from Augustus's daughter
The Senate's demand for a proven general
The disaster in the Teutoburg Forest
questions.explanation: Only when Augustus's two young grandsons, his chosen heirs, had died did he return to Tiberius. He adopted him in AD 4.
questions.sourceQuote: Only after Augustus's two young grandsons and heirs died did the old emperor turn back to him.

questions.question: One modern view holds that Tiberius might be remembered as a model ruler if he had died before which year?
options: AD 26
AD 14
AD 37
AD 19
AD 23
AD 31
questions.explanation: AD 23 is the turning point because that year Tiberius's son died and he came to rely heavily on Sejanus. His overall record was better than his reputation.
questions.sourceQuote: Had he died before AD 23, one modern view holds, he might be remembered as a model ruler.

questions.question: What was unusual about Caligula's accession in AD 37?
options: At 19, he ruled under the praetorian prefect as regent
At 36, the Guard proclaimed him against the Senate's will
At 24, he shared power with Tiberius's grandson for years
At 30, he took power after years commanding the Rhine legions
At 24, he was chosen by the Senate after a month of debate
At 24, with no experience, he got all imperial powers in one day
questions.explanation: Caligula was only 24, had no political or military experience, and received all of an emperor's powers in a single day. He was born in AD 12, the son of Germanicus.
questions.sourceQuote: When Tiberius died in AD 37, Caligula, aged 24 and without political or military experience, received all of an emperor's powers in a single day.

questions.question: What happened to the governor of Syria with whom Germanicus had quarrelled before his death?
options: He was lynched by a mob in Rome
He fled to the Parthians
He was executed on Tiberius's orders
He was acquitted and returned to Syria
He was exiled to Rhodes
He killed himself before his trial ended
questions.explanation: The governor took his own life before his trial was over. Rumours that Tiberius was behind Germanicus's death never went away.
questions.sourceQuote: The governor killed himself before his trial ended, and rumours that Tiberius was behind it all never faded.

questions.question: How was Caligula's memory treated after his murder? (select all that apply)
options: The new emperor refused to condemn his memory
His ashes were thrown into the Tiber
The Senate declared him a god
His assassins were rewarded with high office
Many of his statues were recarved with other faces
He was declared a public enemy
questions.explanation: His uncle, the new emperor, executed the assassins and would not declare Caligula a public enemy or condemn his memory. Even so, many of Caligula's statues were quietly recarved with other emperors' faces.
questions.sourceQuote: The new emperor executed the assassins and refused to declare his nephew a public enemy (*hostis*) or condemn his memory (*damnatio memoriae*).

questions.question: What was Tiberius's situation when Augustus died on 19 August AD 14?
options: He was 55 and living in retirement on Rhodes
He was 48 and campaigning on the Danube
He was 55 and already shared the emperor's powers
He was 77 and serving as sole consul
He was 42 and commanding the Rhine legions
He was 35 and newly adopted as heir
questions.explanation: Tiberius was 55 and already held a share of the emperor's powers. The Senate confirmed him as princeps the following month.
questions.sourceQuote: When Augustus died on 19 August AD 14, Tiberius was 55 and already shared the emperor's powers.

questions.question: What did Sejanus do after Tiberius retired to Capri? (select all that apply)
options: Persuaded the Senate to deify Tiberius
Recovered a lost legionary eagle
Commanded the Rhine legions in Germany
Controlled messages between emperor and capital
Ran the state
Used treason trials to destroy rivals
questions.explanation: With Tiberius away, Sejanus governed, filtered communications and used treason trials against rivals. Germanicus's widow and her two eldest sons were exiled and later died in suspicious circumstances.
questions.sourceQuote: Sejanus ran the state and controlled the messages passing between emperor and capital.

questions.question: Which details suggest that ancient tales of Caligula's financial ruin may be exaggerated? (select all that apply)
options: He refused to use the Guard as tax collectors
Many of his taxes outlived him
He left nearly 3 billion sesterces
He returned estates seized from rich men
His successor seems to have inherited a solvent treasury
He abolished the tax on weddings
questions.explanation: Ancient writers say he squandered a fortune and then taxed everything from weddings to prostitutes. Yet his successor seems to have found a solvent treasury, and many of his taxes stayed in place. The 3 billion sesterces figure belongs to Tiberius.
questions.sourceQuote: Yet his successor seems to have inherited a solvent treasury, and many of the taxes outlived him.
